item.title: Wakayama Castle: Stronghold of a Tokugawa Branch — Guide
item.description: Wakayama Castle stands on Torafusu Hill in the middle of the prefectural capital, founded in 1585 by Toyotomi Hidenaga, brother of Hideyoshi, and later the seat of the Kishu Tokugawa — one of the three branch families of the shogunal house, from which the eighth shogun Yoshimune came. Its keep was destroyed in the war and rebuilt in concrete in 1958, but the extensive stone walls, gates and the winding hilltop layout remain impressive, and the Nishinomaru garden below, with its pond, teahouse and vermilion Ohashi covered bridge, is one of the finest in the region.

item.title: Nagoya Castle: Golden Shachihoko and the Honmaru Palace — Guide
item.description: Nagoya Castle was built on the orders of Tokugawa Ieyasu in 1612 as the seat of the Owari branch of his family, and its keep — crowned with a pair of golden shachihoko, the mythical tiger-headed dolphins that became the symbol of the city — presides over broad moats and massive stone ramparts. The great prize of a visit today is the Honmaru Palace, destroyed in the war and painstakingly rebuilt using original techniques, its chambers lined with dazzling gold-leaf screens of tigers and pines and its fresh hinoki cypress halls among the finest examples of shoin-zukuri palace architecture anywhere in Japan.

item.title: Nijo Castle Guide: The Shogun's Palace & Nightingale Floors
item.description: Nijo Castle is where the power of the shogun was put on display — and, three centuries later, where it was formally surrendered. Built by the Tokugawa shoguns as their Kyoto residence, it is not a fortress of soaring keeps but a sprawling palace of tatami halls, gold-leaf screens, ornate carved transoms, and gardens, surrounded by moats and stone walls. Walking its Ninomaru Palace — across floors deliberately engineered to “sing” like nightingales to warn of intruders — is one of the most evocative historical experiences in Kyoto, and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
